# Agent Brief

This brief explains how agents should use the Genesis founding docs while
working in this repository. It is not a founding doc and it does not replace the
Manifesto, Philosophy, or Principles.

The canonical doctrine stays in the docs. This page is the map for loading and
applying it.

If your agent environment supports local skills, load
`.agents/skills/genesis-doctrine/SKILL.md`. That skill is the executable
protocol for this brief: it tells agents how to select the right canonical docs,
run a light preflight, and use the review rubric.

For research tasks, also load `.agents/skills/genesis-research/SKILL.md` and
use `docs/research/research-standard.md`.

For experiment tasks, use the project-local Experiment Team extension at
`.pi/extensions/experiment-team/`. It is the canonical protocol for creating
experiments, preserving role isolation, writing firewall artifacts, reviewing
bias, running experiments, and updating experiment docs.

For web app tasks, read `apps/web/AGENTS.md` and the nested `AGENTS.md` file for
the area being edited. The web app is the current human-facing Genesis frontend,
not the Genesis kernel.

For consumer UI copy (Settings strings, dialogs, toasts, badges, enum labels),
load `.agents/skills/genesis-ui-copy/SKILL.md` and
`docs/product/web-app/ui-copy.md`.

For production investigations (deployed sessions, org issues, rollout failures),
load `.agents/skills/genesis-investigator/SKILL.md` and follow the narrowest
child skill (`session-investigator`, `org-investigator`, or
`rollout-deployment-investigator`).

## Purpose

Agents working on Genesis should not treat the founding docs as background
reading. They should use them as an operating frame for planning, building, and
reviewing work.

The goal is simple: make product, architecture, implementation, and docs work
line up with what Genesis is.

## Context Map

| Source | Use when | What to take from it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AGENTS.md` | Starting any agent session in this repo | Repo-specific working rules and verification expectations |
| `PRODUCT.md` | Establishing audience, purpose, or tone | Genesis exists first to align builders around doctrine |
| `DESIGN.md` | Changing product design, UX, UI, brand expression, docs style, visuals, or diagrams | The Genesis visual and interaction standard as it evolves |
| [`manifesto.md`](manifesto.md) | Understanding why Genesis exists | The future organization, digital employees, generative kernel, self-similarity, durable capability |
| [`philosophy.md`](philosophy.md) | Making product or architecture decisions | The model: steering, goal-directed work, desired state, recursive operation, memory, oversight, earned autonomy |
| [`principles.md`](principles.md) | Implementing or reviewing work | Decision rules for what to build, defer, expose, and refuse |
| [`writing-standard.md`](writing-standard.md) | Editing docs | Markdown-first writing rules, voice, structure, and verification |
| [`template.md`](template.md) | Creating a new doctrine page | The default page shape for new docs |
| [`research/`](research/) | Creating or updating research | Source-backed product, market, technical, and competitive research |
| [`research/research-standard.md`](research/research-standard.md) | Running research | Placement, source, doctrine, and verification rules for research |
| `.pi/extensions/experiment-team/` | Creating, running, or reviewing Genesis experiments | Role-based experiment protocol, firewall artifacts, bias review, and evidence handoff |
| `apps/web/AGENTS.md` | Changing the Genesis web app | App commands, Agentuity project shape, and the Kernel vs Web App boundary |
| `.github/workflows/genesis-deploy.yml` + `apps/web/scripts/README.md` + `infra/azure/docs/github-oidc.md` | Azure deploy ops (OIDC, path-filtered edge/stable) | Automated on main/release; no dedicated skill |
| [`product/web-app/`](product/web-app/) | Explaining or orienting around the web app | Current app architecture, chat sessions, briefing, files, integrations, design system, and agent guidance |

## Genesis Fit Preflight

For meaningful work, run a light Genesis-fit preflight before editing or
reviewing. Keep it short. Skip it for tiny mechanical changes.

```text
GENESIS_FIT:
goal_or_task:
relevant_principles:
missing_capabilities:
mission_vs_construction:
human_leverage_risk:
reviewability:
```

Use the preflight to decide which doctrine points actually change the work. Do
not list every principle by habit.

## Review Rubric

Use the founding docs as a review rubric. This rubric is a compressed review
lens derived from [`principles.md`](principles.md), not a replacement for it. If
a question changes the review outcome, read the relevant principle before
deciding.

The core questions are:

- Does this build durable capability, or only complete the current task?
- Does it preserve the goal behind the user's request?
- Does it protect human attention, time, budget, and labor?
- Does it make meaningful work legible?
- Does it expose missing capability instead of hiding it?
- Does it separate mission execution from capability construction?
- Does it govern risky action, credentials, budget, and authority explicitly?
- Does durable learning become memory, skill, test, policy, or another reusable artifact?
- Does it keep the hand-written kernel small?
- Does it preserve self-similarity across agents, teams, organizations, and Genesis itself?
- Can the work be reviewed later by humans and agents?

Not every task touches every question. The useful review is the one that finds
the relevant pressure points.

## Working Pattern

1. Read the repo instructions.
2. Load this brief.
3. Load the canonical docs relevant to the task.
4. Run a short Genesis-fit preflight for meaningful work.
5. Build, review, or edit in the smallest useful scope.
6. Validate the work.
7. Report what changed, what was checked, and which doctrine points mattered.

## Non-Goals

- Do not duplicate the founding docs here.
- Do not make agents paste the entire doctrine into every task.
- Do not turn the docs into a pitch deck, command catalog, or generic AI policy.
- Do not create ceremony that slows trivial changes.

## Editing Notes

- Keep this page useful in GitHub.
- Keep the context map current as new canonical docs are added.
- Keep the preflight short enough that agents will actually use it.

# Genesis Doctrine

This skill helps agents apply Genesis doctrine to real work. It does not replace
the founding docs. Treat the docs as canonical and this skill as the operating
protocol for using them.

## Canonical Sources

Always inspect `AGENTS.md` first.

For meaningful Genesis work, read `docs/agent-brief.md`, then load only the
canonical sources that match the task:

| Source | Use when |
| --- | --- |
| `PRODUCT.md` | You need repo purpose, audience, tone, or product context. |
| `DESIGN.md` | You are changing product design, UX, UI, brand expression, docs style, visuals, or diagrams. |
| `docs/manifesto.md` | You need the reason Genesis exists or the core thesis. |
| `docs/philosophy.md` | You need the product and engineering model behind Genesis. |
| `docs/principles.md` | You need decision rules for implementation or review. |
| `docs/writing-standard.md` | You are creating or editing docs. |
| `docs/template.md` | You are creating a new doctrine page. |

Do not paste or rewrite large sections of these docs into new agent-facing
material. Reference the canonical files and preserve them as the source of
truth.

## Genesis Fit Preflight

For non-trivial work, run a light preflight before editing or reviewing. Keep it
short. Skip it for purely mechanical or tiny changes.

```text
GENESIS_FIT:
goal_or_task:
relevant_principles:
missing_capabilities:
mission_vs_construction:
human_leverage_risk:
reviewability:
```

Use the preflight to identify the handful of doctrine points that actually
change the work. If a task conflicts with Genesis doctrine, surface the conflict
before implementing around it.

## Work Protocol

1. Classify the task as docs, product, architecture, code, or review.
2. Load the relevant canonical docs from the context map.
3. Identify the principles that change the plan.
4. Do the smallest scoped work that satisfies the task and preserves doctrine.
5. Validate with the relevant build, test, or static check.
6. In the handoff, mention any doctrine tradeoff, unresolved risk, or standard
   that could not be followed.

## Review Rubric

When reviewing Genesis work, check only the rubric points that apply. This is a
compressed review lens derived from `docs/principles.md`, not a replacement for
the Principles. If a rubric point changes the review outcome, open
`docs/principles.md` and use the canonical principle text before deciding.

- **Durable capability:** Does the work help Genesis do more next time, or only
  produce a one-off result?
- **Goals over tasks:** Does it preserve the user's intended outcome instead of
  forcing the user to decompose every step?
- **Human leverage:** Does it protect attention, time, budget, and labor, or
  create noisy review and low-value interruption?
- **Legibility:** Can a human or agent see who did the work, what authority was
  used, what changed, and what was learned?
- **Missing capability:** Are gaps exposed clearly instead of hidden behind a
  generic assistant surface?
- **Mission versus construction:** Is user-requested work separated from system
  capability-building work?
- **Risk governance:** Are approvals, credentials, irreversible actions,
  external side effects, and budget-sensitive actions explicit?
- **Memory quality:** Does durable learning become structured memory, skill,
  test, policy, or another maintainable artifact?
- **Kernel boundary:** Does the change keep the hand-written kernel small and
  push specialized capability into constructed, registered systems?
- **Self-similarity:** Does the same primitive model work across agents, teams,
  departments, organizations, and Genesis itself?
- **Reviewability:** Does important work leave a trail that humans and agents can
  inspect?

## Handoff

When the work is complete, report:

- What changed.
- What validation ran.
- Which doctrine points mattered, if any.
- Any missing capability or follow-up that should become durable.

**Language** ships with English (`en`, source of truth) and Portuguese Brazil
(`pt-BR`). v1 covers app chrome only — sidebar nav, account menu, settings nav,
connectivity banners, relative date groups, and Appearance controls (`common` and
`shell` namespaces). Mission copy, Hub prompts, and agent skills stay English
until area tickets add namespaces. Detection order: saved locale → browser →
`en`. Developer workflow: `apps/web/src/web/i18n/README.md`.

Color mode, language, and appearance prefs **survive logout** (device-level, not
session-scoped): `ui-theme`, `locale`, `ui-font-size-px`, `reduce-motion`,
`activity-detail`, `voice-input-notice-shown`. There is no
accent palette or color-family selector — only light/dark/system mode.

**Activity detail** defaults to **Compact**. The client sends the preference on
every `sessions.sync`; the server always stores sanitized thinking and tool
invocation events in the sequenced log, but only delivers Intermediate/Verbose
payloads to sockets that opted in (see [Session Message Delivery](session-message-delivery.md)
and [Chat Sessions — Activity detail](chat-sessions.md#activity-detail)).

User-facing labels: [UI Copy — Settings → Appearance](ui-copy.md#settings--appearance).

### Sensitive details in sessions (Appearance)

**Appearance** (`/settings`, Appearance tab) includes **Sensitive details** under
the **Sessions** block, next to **Activity detail**. The control sets how Genesis
handles regex-detected sensitive values (email, phone, payment and government
identifiers, API secrets, and similar patterns) before they reach the Hub.

| API | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /api/settings/pii` | Returns `protectionEnabled` and the saved send policy from the auth session. |
| `PUT /api/settings/pii` | Persists `piiSendPolicy` inside `user_setting.preferences` (JSONB) and refreshes the signed session cookie. |

Policy values are stored under `user_setting.preferences.piiSendPolicy`:

| Stored value | UI label | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `null` | Ask before sending | Inline consent bar on send when sensitive patterns are detected. |
| `mask` | Always mask | Replace detected values with protected tokens before the AI sees them. |
| `off` | Send as typed | Do not mask detected values in new messages. |

---
name: coderabbit-coderabbit-conversations
description: List and resolve all unresolved CodeRabbit review conversations from the current PR
version: "1.0.0"
license: Apache-2.0
allowed-tools: "Bash,Read,edit_file,todo_write"
metadata:
  command: "gh api graphql"
  tags: "github pr review coderabbit"
---

# CodeRabbit Conversations

List all unresolved CodeRabbit review conversations from the current PR, create a TODO list to address each one, and resolve them all once fixed.

## Why GraphQL Instead of REST

The `gh pr view --json reviews,comments` approach only returns review-level data and misses individual conversation threads. GitHub's GraphQL API exposes the `reviewThreads` connection which gives us:

- Per-thread resolution status (`isResolved`)
- Whether the comment is outdated/outside diff (`isOutdated`)
- The exact file path and line number
- The full comment body
- Thread IDs needed for the `resolveReviewThread` mutation

## Scripts

All scripts live in `scripts/` relative to this skill file. Run them from that directory.

| Script | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `get-pr-info.sh` | Exports `PR_NUMBER`, `PR_TITLE`, `PR_URL`, `OWNER`, `REPO` — sourced by the other scripts |
| `list-threads.sh` | Fetches and prints all unresolved CodeRabbit threads for the current PR |
| `resolve-threads.sh` | Resolves all unresolved CodeRabbit threads for the current PR |

## Workflow

### Step 1: List Unresolved Conversations

Run from the repo root (or any directory — the scripts use `gh` context):

```bash
./scripts/list-threads.sh
```

This prints every unresolved, non-outdated CodeRabbit thread with its thread ID, file path, line number, and comment body.

> If the PR has more than 100 threads the script exits with a warning. In that case, use cursor-based pagination with the `after` parameter in the GraphQL query.

### Step 2: Create TODO List

After listing, use `todo_write` to create one TODO item per conversation thread. Each TODO should include:

- The thread ID (needed for resolving later)
- The file path and line number
- A brief summary of the issue

### Step 3: Fix Each Issue

Work through the TODOs:
1. Read the relevant file and understand the issue
2. Make the fix
3. Mark the TODO as completed
4. Move to the next one

### Step 4: Resolve All Conversations

After all fixes are committed, resolve every thread:

```bash
./scripts/resolve-threads.sh
```

## Guidelines

- Always fetch threads via GraphQL, not `gh pr view --json reviews` (which misses thread-level data)
- Only process unresolved, non-outdated threads from `coderabbitai`
- Create one TODO per conversation thread for tracking
- Fix all issues before resolving conversations
- Resolve conversations only after the code changes are committed
- If a thread has more than 100 conversations (unlikely), use cursor-based pagination with the `after` parameter

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Prints PR number, URL, title, repo owner, and repo name as JSON.
# Usage: eval "$(./get-pr-info.sh)"

set -euo pipefail

PR_JSON=$(gh pr view --json number,url,title --jq '{number,url,title}')
REPO_JSON=$(gh repo view --json owner,name --jq '{owner: .owner.login, name: .name}')

---
name: context-management
description: "Use this skill for multi-turn, phased, or noisy work: research/reading, debugging, plan-then-execute, retries/pivots, background or asynchronous work, handoffs, user decisions, task switching, repeated items, or repeated progress checks. It keeps the conversation as a clean working set with checkpoints, timeline review, and compaction at continuation boundaries. Always use when resuming after context compaction or when a long phase reaches a decision, handoff, validation, or task-switch boundary. Usually skip simple one-shot tasks."
---

# Context Management

Use this skill to keep the active conversation as a useful **working set** for the next step. Keep raw only the context that still needs direct reasoning; carry the rest as compact task state when that is more efficient.

Core rhythm:

- **checkpoint before mess**
- **review timeline when structure affects the next decision**
- **compact when a state summary is a better working set than the raw trail**

Use only these tools:

- `context_checkpoint`
- `context_timeline`
- `context_compact`

## Working-set model

Before choosing a tool, ask:

- What am I trying to do next?
- What facts, constraints, or artifacts must stay raw for that next action?
- What important data has a reliable external source I can re-check instead of carrying raw?
- What history is useful only as a conclusion, pointer, or state update?
- What history is process noise or stale baggage?

Classify context into:

- **Raw context:** user intent, constraints, code/log/error details, evidence, or plan text you expect to inspect directly soon.
- **State summary:** decisions, findings, lessons, changed files, validation status, source pointers, rejected leads, and next steps that can replace raw process.
- **Discardable process:** repetitive searches, verbose logs, abandoned hypotheses, false starts, and unrelated turns whose useful value is already captured or gone.

If the active context is already small, coherent, and directly useful for the next step, do not manage it just to be tidy.

## When to use

Use this mode when the work may outgrow one clean thread:

- search, research, browser work, or reading many files/logs/pages/results
- investigate -> decide -> execute -> validate
- plan -> implement -> verify
- background or asynchronous work, handoffs, user decisions, or delayed results
- multiple approaches, retries, failed branches, comparisons, or pivots
- repeated similar cases, tickets, reviews, or batch items
- a main task that may be interrupted by side tasks
- repeated progress/status checks that indicate active state is hard to track
- scattered threads that need cleanup before continuing
- debugging, troubleshooting, refactoring, migration, or code-facing work that may get noisy

If one of these clearly applies, take a structural action now, usually a checkpoint. Do not merely describe the workflow. If the user has not provided enough task details, still checkpoint the workflow shape before asking clarifying questions.

Usually skip this skill for one-shot reads, bounded summaries, direct rewrites, simple lookups, deterministic scripts, short tasks that can stay clean, or moments where the active context is already a good working set.

## Start-of-turn check

At the start of each new user message, classify it:

- **Same task / next phase:** continue; if the previous phase is complete and noisy, compact before the next phase.
- **Correction or follow-up:** usually answer from recent context; do not compact yet.
- **New task or direction shift:** if the previous task left a complete noisy segment, inspect timeline when anchors are unclear, then compact to a continuation anchor that gives the new task a clean working set.

Think of the tools as a phase pipeline: checkpoint marks anchors, work happens, timeline shows structure, and compact creates a new branch from the chosen continuation anchor with a summary of what happened after it. The target is a working-set choice, not an age choice.

## Main loop

1. Before noisy work, create a semantic checkpoint as the first context-management action. If the first job is orientation over existing history, run `context_timeline` before adding a new checkpoint.
2. When the task shape is clear, read one matching scenario reference only if it will change tool timing, anchor choice, or summary content. Skip reference loading for obvious short applications where this main skill body is enough.
3. Add checkpoints at meaningful milestones: phase boundaries, risky attempts, reusable batch methods, and interruptions.
4. Use `context_timeline` when the active path structure affects the next decision or compact target.
5. At continuation boundaries, run the compact gate before starting another phase. If the whole requested task is complete and only the final response remains, answer and wait.
6. After a successful compact, continue from the injected summary instead of dragging the full raw path forward.

## Continuation boundaries

A continuation boundary is a point where the current phase has produced a stable result and the next action will use that result to start a different phase. It is not necessarily the end of the user's whole task.

Examples: investigation -> decision/plan/implementation, implementation -> validation, failed validation -> next approach, delayed result -> routing/action, user decision -> execution, rejected branch -> replacement direction, side request -> pause/summarize mainline before switching.

Do not ask only "is the whole task done?" Ask "will the next action start a new phase using the stable result of this phase?" If yes, this is often a compaction boundary.

Handoffs are not final answers: if a response transfers control to the user, another actor/process, later validation, or a queued phase, compact when the prior phase was noisy and the next action needs only stable state.

## Read the right reference

Read **one primary reference** only when the scenario pattern will affect tool timing, anchor choice, or summary content:

- search / research / reading-heavy work -> `references/search-research-and-reading.md`
- development / debugging / troubleshooting / refactoring / migration -> `references/development-and-troubleshooting.md`
- planning / staged execution / todo-driven work -> `references/planning-and-execution.md`
- repeated similar items / batch work -> `references/repeated-items-and-batch-work.md`
- task switching / pause-resume / interruptions / cleanup-and-continue -> `references/task-switching-and-cleanup.md`
- interleaved async work / overlapping fronts / background results / user decisions -> `references/interleaved-async-work.md`

Also read `references/retry-branch-and-pivot.md` when multiple approaches, failed branches, comparisons, retries, or pivots become central.

## Tool policy

### `context_checkpoint`

Use before noisy work, a new phase, a risky attempt, switching subtasks, or after a meaningful milestone. Use semantic names such as `<task>-start`, `<task>-<phase>`, `<task>-<attempt>`, or `<task>-<milestone>`. Avoid generic names like `start`, `checkpoint-1`, or `retry`.

### `context_timeline`

Use it as the structural view of the active path:

- when the current path shape affects the next decision
- when several checkpoints, branches, or task switches exist
- before choosing a non-obvious compact target
- when the thread feels cluttered and you need to distinguish useful context from baggage

When reading the timeline, ask which raw messages are still needed for the immediate next action, which paths are now baggage, and which anchor gives the smallest sufficient working set after summary injection.

### `context_compact`

Use it to replace raw history with a state summary when the next phase would benefit from a smaller working set.

Typical compact boundaries: investigation -> execution, diagnosis -> fix, implementation -> validation, failed attempt -> next attempt, representative item -> remaining batch, completed noisy task -> new user task.

Strong signals to consider compaction:

- repeated progress/status checks
- inability to summarize current state, next action, and open risks in one short paragraph
- rejected, abandoned, or superseded branches
- stable result after many tool calls or long output
- returned background/asynchronous/delegated result
- material plan or approach change
- side question arriving while stale process history is active

Do not compact while exploration is still active, when the result is unstable, just because the skill triggered, or just because the user-visible task ended.

## Compact gate

Before calling `context_compact`, require all three:

1. The segment being left behind is noisy, stale, failed, low-value in raw form, or actively reducing focus.
2. You can restore the useful task state in a clear summary.
3. There is an immediate continuation that benefits from cleaner context.

If the compact is prompted by a new user message, a direction shift, or several possible checkpoint targets, run `context_timeline` first and choose the target from visible structure rather than memory.

If the whole task is done and only the final answer remains, wait. Compact later only if the next user message makes it useful.

Checkpoint-only failure mode: a checkpoint is useful because it gives you a clean anchor to compact back to later. After any checkpointed phase produces a stable result, ask what the phase settled, whether the next step is different, and whether a summary can replace the raw trail. If yes, compact; do not keep accumulating raw history just because the overall task is still active.

## Choosing target and backup

Choose the continuation anchor by designing the next working set:

1. Name the immediate next action.
2. Decide what must remain raw: active user intent, current constraints, still-open evidence/code context, an approved plan being executed, or details you expect to inspect directly next.
3. Decide what can become state summary or disappear: completed searches, verbose logs, failed attempts, stale branches, earlier unrelated tasks, externally recoverable data, and clear process details.
4. Pick the anchor that leaves the new branch with the **smallest sufficient context** after summary injection.
5. If an older anchor plus a stronger summary is cleaner than a recent anchor plus stale context, prefer the older anchor. When completed fronts fill the middle of the thread, it can be correct to compact to a much older anchor or even `root` if the summary restores the active front and source pointers.

Avoid targets that are too late, too early with a weak summary, or semantically wrong. If there are several checkpoints, a task switch, or uncertainty about the best working set, run `context_timeline` first.

Use `backupCheckpoint` when raw history may still matter later. A backup is a recovery safety net, not a substitute for the summary.

## Compact summary contract

The summary is not a transcript recap. It is the state needed to resume work from the chosen anchor; older or cleaner anchors require stronger summaries.

Context tools change conversation state, not the outside world. Files, processes, browser state, tickets, databases, remote services, and other side effects stay current. If you compact to an anchor before those changes, the summary must bridge the gap between old conversation context and current external state.

A compact summary must restore:

1. **Task state:** current task, user intent, constraints, decisions, assumptions, and known result/progress/failure.
2. **External state:** changed files, created/deleted artifacts, running/stopped processes, browser actions, tickets/records, deployments, remote changes.
3. **Verification state:** commands already run, validation status, notable outputs, and remaining risks or open questions.
4. **Navigation state:** source anchors/evidence when needed, rejected leads worth avoiding, backup checkpoint guidance, and explicit next step.

If important data has a reliable external source, preserve the pointer and retrieval method rather than copying the raw data. Examples: file path and line/query, database table/query, task/job id, log path, URL, record id, branch/commit, or command to inspect status. Include raw values only when they are small, unstable, hard to retrieve, or needed for immediate reasoning.

For long-running work, shape the summary as a state capsule: goal, stable result, decisions, rejected paths, current artifacts/source pointers, active work, pending input, risks/open questions, and next action. Include why compacting is appropriate only when it helps future orientation. Avoid vague summaries like `Done`, `Investigated`, `Switching context`, or `Going back`.

Before compacting, quickly check: stable state? real continuation? smallest sufficient working set? summary restores state after the anchor? externally recoverable data represented by pointers? external side effects and validation captured? explicit next step?

## After compact

1. Read the injected summary carefully and treat it as the new active state.
2. Verify it contains enough state for the next action.
3. Remember that disk and external systems were not rolled back; inspect current files/tools/services when state matters.
4. If a missing detail is cheap to reconstruct from disk, tools, or source anchors, retrieve it directly.
5. Return to the backup checkpoint only when the missing raw context cannot be reconstructed cheaply.

## Common mistakes

Avoid:

- checkpointing constantly without phase meaning
- checkpointing early but never compacting after a stable phase result
- compacting blindly without timeline when anchor choice is unclear
- preserving too much raw history because older anchors or `root` feel risky
- using an old anchor or `root` with a weak summary
- compacting immediately after a final deliverable when no next user intent is known
- carrying completed noisy phases into a new task
- treating handoff or decision prompts as final answers when a continuation is expected
- writing summaries that recap history but fail to restore current task state
- assuming compact or branch navigation reverts files, processes, browser state, or remote services
- omitting decisions, constraints, external side effects, changed files, validation status, or next step

**Analyzing i18n tasks**

I’m wondering why there might be stale checks or if things have shifted. We’ve had a clean slate before. It seems like we need to address what's left for internationalization (i18n) in the app. We should clarify our definition of "done," focusing on the first locale, pt-BR, while noting that model-generated content and RTL are beyond scope. 

I might list tasks in priority:
1. Merge PR #1262.
2. Rebuild onboarding/auth for current onboarding-v2. 
3. Complete various area tickets. 
4. Finish the settings tracker and audit strings.

**Considering app-wide QA**

I’m focusing on app-wide QA and hardening tasks. First, there's an automated audit for hardcoded UI strings, which lacks a guard beyond parity. I need to address locale parity, pluralization, and formatting, especially for PT-BR across various routes.

Next, I should update ticket statuses and close the epic. Merging the epic might require expanding documentation, but we need to verify if potential auth routes are outside the app. I also need to note that the old TAC-684 commit can't be replayed due to architecture changes, which affects localization. Code looks implemented in the PR, but the ticket is still in progress and needs closure after merging.

**Evaluating untranslated strings**

I’m considering the possibility that there might still be untranslated settings strings identified by CodeRabbit. While we've fixed security issues, there could still be raw strings in the broader settings. Am I sure we've addressed everything? The user wants to know what’s left. 

It seems we should audit the code for hardcoded English, though this could be a massive task. I can frame it as "according to Linear and the current PR, a route-level audit is still necessary." We could also check namespace registrations for common areas like shell, sessions, and settings, but collections and teams appear absent. The i18n README mentions planned namespaces for areas.

content.text:
Short version: **PR #1262 is ready, but app-wide i18n is not complete.** The branch currently has only four app namespaces: `common`, `shell`, `sessions`, and `settings`.

## Remaining product areas

| Ticket | Area | Actual state |
|---|---|---|
| [TAC-679](https://linear.app/agentuity/issue/TAC-679/i18n-collections) | Collections | In Progress; not included in PR #1262 |
| [TAC-680](https://linear.app/agentuity/issue/TAC-680/i18n-apps-and-builders) | Apps and builders | In Progress; not included in PR #1262 |
| [TAC-681](https://linear.app/agentuity/issue/TAC-681/i18n-teams-and-organization) | Teams and organization | Todo |
| [TAC-683](https://linear.app/agentuity/issue/TAC-683/i18n-capabilities) | Capabilities | Todo |
| [TAC-685](https://linear.app/agentuity/issue/TAC-685/i18n-presentations-ads-files-and-misc-pages) | Presentations, ads, files, agents, help, releases, sharing | Todo |

## Work that needs reconciliation

- **TAC-684 — onboarding and auth** is marked Done, but its old implementation targeted components replaced by onboarding-v2 and was intentionally omitted from PR #1262.
  - Reimplement onboarding localization against the current flow.
  - Audit `/switch-org`, `/desktop-auth-return`, first-run states, and auth-adjacent public-shell copy.

- **TAC-682 — settings/connections** is still marked In Progress.
  - Its implementation is now in PR #1262.
  - After acceptance testing and merge, update/close the ticket.

## Final completion work

1. Merge [PR #1262](https://github.com/agentuity/genesis-mono/pull/1262).
2. Complete the five untranslated product-area tickets above.
3. Redo onboarding/auth localization for the current architecture.
4. Run an app-wide hardcoded-string audit, covering:
   - Buttons, dialogs, toasts, validation and accessibility labels
   - Empty/loading/error states
   - Dates, times, numbers, plurals, and dynamic fallback messages
5. Perform English and pt-BR route-by-route QA on desktop and mobile.
6. Verify locale persistence, browser detection, fallback behavior, and deep links.
7. Update the stale Linear statuses and close parent epic [TAC-675](https://linear.app/agentuity/issue/TAC-675/add-internationalization-i18n-to-genesis).

Already substantially complete: the framework, shared shell/navigation, sessions/chat, settings/connections, and public website. Model-generated chat translation, RTL polish, and desktop-specific packaging remain explicitly out of the current epic’s scope.
